bullets.text: Machine Learning (ML) is a fast-growing area in technology.
ML is a subfield of Artificial Intelligence (AI), which aims to simulate human intelligence.
ML systems learn patterns from data to make decisions or predictions, rather than being explicitly programmed.
Models improve over time with more data without needing reprogramming.
Machine learning is integrated into many aspects of daily life.
Examples include Netflix recommendations and email spam filters.
Other applications: virtual assistants (Siri/Alexa), facial recognition, and fraud detection.
ML's popularity is due to major developments over the last decade.
Access to vast amounts of data from various sources (social media, web searches).
Increased computational power, thanks to modern hardware like GPUs.
Development of sophisticated algorithms that extract insights more effectively.
The most common type of ML, especially in industry applications.
Models are trained using labeled data, where each input has a correct output.
Goal is to predict outputs for new, unseen inputs based on learned relationships.
Example: Predicting house prices based on features and actual sale prices.
Problems are categorized into Regression (predicting continuous values) and Classification (predicting discrete labels).
Uses unlabeled data, meaning only inputs are provided without explicit answers.
Algorithms discover patterns, relationships, or structures in the data independently.
Clustering is a common application, grouping similar data points (e.g., customer segments).
Dimensionality reduction techniques simplify datasets with many features.
An agent learns by interacting with an environment.
Decisions lead to feedback in the form of rewards or penalties.
The goal is to learn a policy that maximizes total reward over time.
Examples include training robots to walk or AI playing games like chess (AlphaGo).
ML is powerful but faces challenges; it is not magic.
Data quality is crucial: noisy, biased, or incomplete data harms model performance.
Overfitting occurs when a model learns training data too well but fails to generalize to new data.
Ethical concerns are prominent, as biased data can lead to biased models with serious real-world consequences.
Recap of ML definition, importance, three main types, and challenges.
Future lectures will delve deeper into each ML type and associated algorithms.
